Dependable AIthe theme

About: Hosted by Hong Kong Science & Technology Parks (HKSTP), the workshop gathered systems- and software-engineering researchers on making complex intelligent systems dependable and trustworthy.

Classical dependability tools are being combined with data-driven methods (LLMs, RL, Gaussian processes); distribution shift and uncertainty recur across control, testing and LLM talks; and trustworthiness — safety, reliability, fairness, explainability — is treated as the gate for deploying AI.

Insight 01 · Dependability & reliability modeling

Reliability & Availability Modeling of Complex Systems in Practice

Dependability modeling · RBD · fault trees · Markov chains
Dependability fundamentals
  • Dependability = justified reliance on the delivered service; a taxonomy of Attributes (availability, reliability, safety, maintainability), Means and Threats
  • The causal chain Fault → Error → Failure
  • Four means: fault prevention, removal (debugging), tolerance (redundancy), forecasting
Quantitative assessment
  • Data-driven vs model-driven paths; discrete-event vs analytic simulation; prefer a numerical solution over simulation when feasible
  • Complexity dimensions: huge models (100s–1000s of components), user-oriented measures, non-exponential distributions (SMP, MRGP), performability
Methods & state-space explosion
  • Simple methods (RBD, fault trees, reliability graphs) assume independence — fast but miss dependencies (shared repair, spares, imperfect coverage)
  • State-space methods (DTMC/CTMC, SMP, phase-type) capture dependency but explode; mitigate via hierarchical composition or fixed-point iteration
Case study — IBM HA SIP
  • A high-availability SIP system on IBM BladeCenter + WebSphere for a telco customer
  • Quantify steady-state availability and a user-oriented DPM (defects-per-million) metric
[1] “Reliability and Availability Modeling of Complex Systems in Practice,” HKSTP Systems Engineering Workshop, 2024.
Insight 02 · Dependability & reliability modeling

Early Detection of Degraded Systems: Self-Healing with Time Delay

Hoang Pham · Rutgers University
Why degradation matters
  • Many systems degrade rather than fail outright; the danger is a degraded-but-undetected state revealed only after a random delay
  • Scale: a 10,000-machine data center sees ~1,000 crashes/day; ~4% of machines hit undetected errors (Google)
Reliability model with delay
  • Reliability R(t) = P1(t) + P2(t): operating normally OR degraded-but-undetected; availability sums the available states
  • A self-healing / self-repair state diagram with delayed, dependent transitions (Pham, IEEE Trans. Reliability, 2024)
A biological analogue
  • Models Healthy cells (H), Infected cells (I) and Virus (V) with delayed transitions — a self-healing analogy
[2] H. Pham, “Early Detection of Degraded Complex Systems: Self-Healing in Uncertain Situations with Time Delay,” HKSTP SE Workshop, 2024.
Insight 03 · Testing, verification & formal methods

Combinatorial Testing for Complex Systems

W. Eric Wong · University of Texas at Dallas
Method: CT + RBD + BVA
  • Security attributes differ from reliability (vulnerability vs probability of failure-free operation)
  • Combine Combinatorial Testing with Reliability-Block-Diagram structure and Boundary Value Analysis to generate efficient test cases
Results
  • Across packages, combinatorial coverage finds more — and different — bugs with fewer test cases than exhaustive runs
  • Claimed ~50% less development and ~90% less maintenance effort for autonomous-system assurance
Depends on the input model
  • Effectiveness hinges on input-space model quality: number of parameters, values per parameter, cases generated, bugs detected
  • AV example: primary vs backup sensors, emergency braking, ‘abnormal sensor’ cases, sun glare, and expansion paths
[3] W. E. Wong, “Combinatorial Testing for Complex Systems: Functional and Non-Functional Perspectives,” HKSTP SE Workshop, 2024.
Insight 04 · Testing, verification & formal methods

Trusted AI & Probabilistic Model Checking

Jin-Song Dong · National University of Singapore
AI failures → formal methods
  • AI has big wins but costly, unexplained failures (Knight Capital, Microsoft Tay, Tesla/Amazon incidents)
  • Model checking works: 2007 ACM Turing Award; Microsoft SLAM finds Windows driver bugs; the PAT toolkit has 400k+ downloads
Probabilistic model checking
  • PMC computes system reliability from component reliability; here applied to sports-winning probability
  • ‘Tennis strategy is an MDP’ (ICDCS 2015): compute winning probability and the optimal strategy
LLMs in the loop
  • A GPT-4 sports-analytics pipeline: video statistics → vision-language extraction → model processor → outcome prediction and strategy
[4] J.-S. Dong, “Trusted AI and Beyond: ChatGPT Reasoning with Sport Analytics Application,” HKSTP SE Workshop, 2024.
Insight 05 · Trustworthy & cognitive AI

From Trustworthy Systems to Trustworthy AI

Xin Yao · trustworthy & evolutionary AI
Trust & requirements
  • Trust and trustworthiness are asymmetrically bidirectional, context-dependent and learnable
  • Six attributes of trustworthy systems: resilience, security, privacy, safety, reliability, availability
Trustworthy & fair AI
  • AI ethics is hierarchical (individual / society / environment); map each principle to a technique — transparency→explainable AI, fairness→fair AI, non-maleficence→safe/robust AI, privacy→federated/differential learning
  • 20+ fairness metrics in five families; feature-attribution explanations judged by faithfulness, sensitivity and complexity
An evolutionary approach
  • A multi-objective evolutionary method (MOFAE) optimizes explanations across metrics; evolutionary constrained learning regulates ML behavior
  • Evolutionary computation is a promising engine for fair, explainable and safe AI
[5] X. Yao, “From Trustworthy Systems to Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence,” HKSTP SE Workshop, 2024.
Insight 06 · Trustworthy & cognitive AI

Data-centric Quality Assurance for AI & LLM Systems

Fujitsu / SEI · data-centric AI quality assurance
A new AI-system paradigm
  • Modern AI systems combine 30+ AI models and 50+ traditional components (e.g. STT → NLP intent → response generation → TTS); a ‘Universal AI-CPS’ on NVIDIA Omniverse
  • ISR-LLM: an iterative self-refined LLM for long-horizon task planning (ICRA 2024)
  • Behavior is learned, not specified → explainability is key and new QA methods are needed
Three core directions
  • Unit level: quality across the ML lifecycle; DeepGauge test-coverage criteria; data-centric out-of-distribution & uncertainty analysis
  • System level: quality assurance and reliability support at integration and system stages
  • Human-centered, explainable MLSysOps across data, model, code and system
GenAI / LLM assurance
  • LLM trustworthiness is at a very early stage; internals are hard to test and debug
  • Tools: the LUNA model-analysis framework; LLM-agent orchestration decomposed into Profile, Memory, Planning and Action
[6] “Data-centric Quality Assurance for Trustworthy AI and LLM Systems,” HKSTP SE Workshop, 2024 (Fujitsu / SEI).
Insight 07 · Trustworthy & cognitive AI

System Science & Autonomous AI Systems

Yingxu Wang · University of Calgary
A hyperstructural model
  • A formal abstract system S ≜ (C, B, Rᶜ, Rᵇ, Rᶠ, Rⁱ, Rᵒ): components, behaviors and internal/external relation sets
  • Abstract intelligence transfers information / knowledge into behavior
Autonomy classification
  • System autonomy by cognitive × behavioral axes: reflexive, imperative, adaptive, autonomous — autonomous intelligence is the 4th (quaternary) level
  • Machine thinking via LRMB (Layered Reference Model of the Brain): sensation, action, perception, memory, cognition, inference, intelligence
Trustworthiness of autonomous systems
  • A tripartite model: structural, behavioral and dynamic trustworthiness
  • A formal model links levels of system intelligence by inclusion
[7] Y. Wang, “System Science and Autonomous AI Systems,” HKSTP SE Workshop, 2024.
Insight 08 · Autonomous systems in the real world

Ensuring Reliability of Autonomous Vehicular Systems

Jianping Wang · City University of Hong Kong
Architecture & vulnerabilities
  • The AD stack on a driving OS (Apollo 3.5/5.0): perception → localization → prediction → planning → control
  • Vulnerabilities: perception-model uncertainty, dynamic per-module compute time, and adverse weather (fog/rain/snow degrade cameras, LiDAR and comms)
Countermeasures by layer
  • Hardware limits → edge computing; software (model uncertainty, timing) → digital twins & cooperative sensing
  • Attacks (physical / adversarial / cyber) → robust driving; adverse weather → robust V2X
Robust driving & scheduling
  • Adversarial-attack-aware motion planning stays safe where naive planning fails; multi-agent prediction + camera/LiDAR/radar fusion handle occlusion
  • Onboard scheduling uses an Age-of-Information metric and an RL agent (reward ∝ 1/AoI), improving miss ratio and response vs Apollo baselines
[8] J. Wang, “Ensuring Reliability of Autonomous Vehicular Systems and Beyond,” HKSTP SE Workshop, 2024.
Insight 09 · Autonomous systems in the real world

Safe Learning for Autonomous Systems

Naira Hovakimyan · University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign
Control theory vs ML
  • Safety-critical systems need guarantees because failures can be deadly; safely obtaining training data is hard
  • Control-theoretic tools (structured, deterministic) are strong on safety/robustness; ML tools (general, stochastic) are strong on empirical performance
Distributional robustness
  • Train-vs-real distribution shift can break the control objective; control the size of the guaranteed set, or be agnostic to the training distribution
  • Distributionally robust optimization with finite samples; verified by Monte-Carlo; incremental stochastic stability
L1 adaptive control + learning
  • L1 adaptive control gives guaranteed uniform performance bounds, decoupling estimation from control (small-gain + Lyapunov)
  • Commercialized with NASA, Caterpillar and JOUAV; extended via contraction metrics, L1-MPC, and contraction-L1 with Gaussian-process learning
[9] N. Hovakimyan, “Safe Learning for Autonomous Systems,” HKSTP SE Workshop, 2024.
Insight 10 · Autonomous systems in the real world

Digital Twins for Complex Systems

Ajith Parlikad · University of Cambridge
What a digital twin is
  • An integrated multi-physics, multi-scale, probabilistic simulation updated by sensors (NASA 2012); a digital replica that improves decision-making (CDBB 2018)
  • A twin should see, learn, think, act, communicate, cooperate and achieve
Collaborative twins
  • Connected assets help each other ‘in times of trouble’ via shared information / computation — faster, coordinated recovery
  • Spans robotics, AI, V2X, perception and blockchain across cyber-physical and cyber-cyber systems
Real cases
  • Japan’s FUKUI self-driving public transit; an Oct 2023 incident where an AV failed to stop and collided, triggering new safety measures
[10] A. Parlikad, “Digital Twins for Complex Systems,” HKSTP SE Workshop, 2024.
Insight 11 · Autonomous systems in the real world

Artificial Intuition, Research Portfolios & Decision Systems

Andrea Belz · research-portfolio analytics
Find the tech before investing
  • An NLP pipeline compiles and augments abstracts, clusters research portfolios, then evaluates clusters and removes redundancy
  • Pipeline: documents → YAKE keywords → Mistral-7B metadata → Sentence-Transformer embeddings → labeled clusters (optics, flight system, remote sensing…)
Choosing the number of clusters
  • Too few clusters = poor coverage; too many = overlap
  • A new redundancy measure R = max cosine similarity between label vectors, plotted vs the number of clusters to pick the knee
Using the labels
  • A k×ĉ coverage matrix yields coverage scores / predicted labels when similarity exceeds a threshold (MMR)
[11] A. Belz, “Artificial Intuition, Research Portfolios and Decision Systems,” HKSTP SE Workshop, 2024.
Conclusions

Synthesis across the workshop

Trends

  • Classical dependability tools (RBD, fault trees, Markov chains, combinatorial testing, probabilistic model checking) are being combined with data-driven methods — not replaced.
  • Distribution shift and uncertainty quantification recur across the control, testing and LLM talks.
  • Autonomous driving is the shared case study grounding abstract reliability and safety methods.

Vision

  • Trustworthiness — resilience, security, privacy, safety, reliability, availability, fairness, explainability — is the gate for deploying AI.
  • Self-aware, cooperative systems: self-healing degradation, cognitive autonomy models, and collaborative digital twins.
  • Formal and guaranteed methods (L1 control, model checking) scaled to data-driven systems.

Implications for us

  • Treat explainability and formal / guaranteed methods as prerequisites, not add-ons (L1 guarantees, PAT/SLAM, DeepGauge, LUNA).
  • Govern the ML lifecycle with data-centric quality assurance and out-of-distribution analysis.
  • GenAI / LLM assurance is immature — the biggest open frontier is testing agentic systems whose behavior is learned, not specified.
